  :2399: p20.2 (402)             20.1. QUANTUM WEIRDNESS
  :2400: 
  :2401: 20.1 Quantum weirdness
  :2402: 
  :2403: It is beyond this book (and its authors) to fully survey quantum mechanics. Fortunately, only
  :2404: very little physics is needed to understand the main results of quantum computing. However,
  :2405: these results do use some of the more counterintuitive notions of quantum mechanics such as the
  :2406: following:
  :2407: 
  :2408: Any object in the universe, whether it is a particle or a cat, does not have definite
  :2409: properties (such as location, state, etc..) but rather has a kind of probability wave over
  :2410: its potential properties. The object only achieves a definite property when it is observed,
  :2411: at which point we say that the probability wave collapses to a single value.
  :2412: 
  :2413: At first this may seem like philosophical pontification analogous to questions such as "if a tree
  :2414: falls and no one hears, does it make a sound?" but these probability waves are in fact very real, in
  :2415: the sense that they can interact and interfere with one another, creating experimentally measurable
  :2416: effects. Below we describe two of the experiments that led physicists to accept this counterintuitive
  :2417: theory.
  :2418: 
  :2419: 20.1.1 The 2-slit experiment
  :2420: 
  :2421: In the 2-slit experiment a source that fires electrons one by one (say, at the rate of one electron per
  :2422: second) is placed in front of a wall containing two tiny slits (see Figure ??). Beyond the wall we
  :2423: place an array of detectors that light up whenever an electron hits them. We measure the number
  :2424: of times each detector lights up during an hour.
  :2425: 
  :2426: When we cover one of the slits, we would expect that the detectors that are directly behind the
  :2427: open slit will receive the largest number of hits, and as Figure ?? shows, this is indeed the case.
  :2428: When both slits are uncovered we expect that the number of times each detector is hit is the sum
  :2429: of the number of times it is hit when the first slit is open and the number of times it is hit when the
  :2430: second slit is open. In particular, uncovering both slits should only increase the number of times
  :2431: each location is hit.
  :2432: 
  :2433: Surprisingly, this is not what happens. The pattern of hits exhibits the "interference" phenom-
  :2434: ena depicted in Figure ??. In particular, at several detectors the total electron flux is lower when
  :2435: both slits are open as compared to when a single slit is open. This defies explanation if electrons
  :2436: behave as particles or "little balls".
  :2437: 
  :2438: According to Quantum mechanics, the explanation is that it is wrong to think of an electron has
  :2439: a "little ball" that can either go through the first slit or the second (i.e., has a definite property).
  :2440: Rather, somehow the electron instantaneously explores all possible paths to the detectors (and so
  :2441: "finds out" how many slits are open) and then decides on a distribution among the possible paths
  :2442: that it will take.
  :2443: 
  :2444: You might be curious to see this "path exploration" in action, and so place a detector at each
  :2445: slit that light up whenever an electron passes through that slit. When this is done, one can see
  :2446: that every electron passes through only one of the slits like a nice little ball. But furthermore, the
  :2447: interference phenomenon disappears and the graph of electron hits becomes, as originally expected,
  :2448: 
  :2449: DRAFT the sum of the hits when each slit is open. The explanation is that, as stated above, observing an
  :2450: Web draft 2007-01-08 21:59
  :2451: 
  :2452: 20.1. QUANTUM WEIRDNESS                                  p20.3 (403)
  :2453: Note 20.1 (Physically implementing quantum computers.)
  :2454: 
  :2455: object "collapses" their distribution of possibilities, and so changes the result of the experiment.
  :2456: (One moral to draw from this is that quantum computers, if they are ever built, will have to be
  :2457: carefully isolated from external influences and noise, since noise may be viewed as a "measurement"
  :2458: performed by the environment on the system. Of course, we can never completely isolate the system,
  :2459: which means we have to make quantum computation tolerant of a little noise. This seems to be
  :2460: possible under some noise models, see the chapter notes.)
  :2461: 
  :2462: 20.1.2 Quantum entanglement and the Bell inequalities.
  :2463: 
  :2464: Even after seeing the results of the 2-slit experiment, you might still be quite skeptical of the
  :2465: explanation that quantum mechanics offers. If you do, you are in excellent company. Albert
  :2466: Einstein didn't buy it either. While he agreed that the 2-slit experiment means that electrons
  :2467: are not exactly "little balls", he didn't think that it is sufficient reason to give up such basic
  :2468: notions of physics such as the existence of an independent reality, with objects having definite
  :2469: properties that do not depend on whether one is observing them. To show the dangerous outcomes
  :2470: of giving up such notions, in a 1951 paper with Podosky and Rosen (EPR for short) he described a
  :2471: thought experiment showing that accepting Quantum mechanics leads to the seemingly completely
  :2472: ridiculous conclusion that systems in two far corners of the universe can instantaneously coordinate
  :2473: their actions.
  :2474: 
  :2475: In 1964 John Bell showed how the principles behind EPR thought experiment can be turned into
  :2476: an actual experiment. In the years since, Bell's experiment has been repeated again and again with
  :2477: the same results: quantum mechanics' predictions were verified and, contrary to Einstein's expec-
  :2478: tations, the experiments refuted his intuitions about how the universe operates. In an interesting
  :2479: twist, in recent years the ideas behind EPR's and Bell's experiments were used for a practical goal:
  :2480: encryption schemes whose security depends only on the principles of quantum mechanics, rather
  :2481: than any unproven conjectures such as P = NP.
  :2482: 
  :2483: For complexity theorists, probably the best way to understand Bell's experiment is as a two
  :2484: prover game. Recall that in the two prover setting, two provers are allowed to decide on a strategy
  :2485: and then interact separately with a polynomial-time verifier which then decides whether to accept
  :2486: or reject the interaction (see Chapters 8 and 18). The provers' strategy can involve arbitrary
  :2487: computation and even be randomized, with the only constraint being that the provers are not
  :2488: allowed to communicate during their interaction with the verifier.
  :2489: 
  :2490: Bell's game. In Bell's setting, we have an extremely simple interaction between the verifier and
  :2491: two provers (that we'll name Alice and Bob): there is no statement that is being proven, and all the
  :2492: communication involves the verifier sending and receiving one bit from each prover. The protocol
  :2493: 
  :2494: DRAFT is as follows:
  :2495: Web draft 2007-01-08 21:59
  :2496: 
  :2497: p20.4 (404)                                                  20.1. QUANTUM WEIRDNESS
  :2498: 
  :2499: 1. The verifier chooses two random bits x, y R {0, 1}.
  :2500: 2. It sends x to Alice and y to Bob.
  :2501: 
  :2502: 3. Let a denote Alice's answer and b Bob's answer.
  :2503: 
  :2504: 4. The verifier accepts if and only if a  b = x  y.
  :2505: 
  :2506: It is easy for Alice and Bob to ensure the verifier accepts with probability 3/4 (e.g., by always
  :2507: sending a = b = 0). It turns out this is the best they can do:
  :2508: 
  :2509: Theorem 20.2 ([Bel64])
  :2510: Regardless of the strategy the provers use, the verifier will accept with probability at most 3/4.
  :2511: 
  :2512: Proof: Assume for the sake of contradiction that there is a (possibly probabilistic) strategy that
  :2513: causes the verifier to accept with probability more than 3/4. By a standard averaging argument
  :2514: there is a fixed set of provers' coins (and hence a deterministic strategy) that causes the verifier to
  :2515: accept with at least the same probability, and hence we may assume without loss of generality that
  :2516: the provers' strategy is deterministic.
  :2517: 
  :2518: A deterministic strategy for the two provers is a pair of functions f, g : {0, 1}  {0, 1} such as
  :2519: the provers' answers a, b are computed as a = f (x) and b = g(y). The function f can be one of only
  :2520: four possible functions: it can be either the constant function zero or one, the function f (x) = x
  :2521: or the function f (y) = 1 - y. We analyze the case that f (x) = x; the other case are similar.
  :2522: 
  :2523: If f (x) = x then the verifier accepts iff b = (x  y)  x. On input y, Bob needs to find b that
  :2524: makes the verifier accept. If y = 1 then x  y = x and hence b = 0 will ensure the verifier accepts
  :2525: with probability 1. However, if y = 0 then (x  y)  x = x and since Bob does not know x, the
  :2526: probability that his output b is equal to x is at most 1/2. Thus the total acceptance probability is
  :2527: at most 3/4.
  :2528: 
  :2529: What does this game have to do with quantum mechanics? The main point is that according
  :2530: 
  :2531: to "classical" pre-quantum physics, it is possible to ensure that Alice and Bob are isolated from
  :2532: 
  :2533: one another. Suppose that you are given a pair of boxes that implement some arbitrary strategy
  :2534: 
  :2535: for Bell's game. How can you ensure that these boxes don't have some secret communication
  :2536: 
  :2537: mechanism that allows them to coordinate their answers? We might try to enclose the devices
  :2538: 
  :2539: in lead boxes, but even this does not ensure complete isolation. However, Einstein's theory of
  :2540: 
  :2541: relativity allows us a foolproof way to ensure complete isolation: place the two devices very far
  :2542: 
  :2543: apart (say at a distance of a 1000 miles from one another), and perform the interaction with each
  :2544: 
  :2545: prover at a breakneck speed: toss each of the coins x, y and demand the answer within less than
  :2546: 
  :2547: one millisecond. Since according to the theory of relativity, nothing travels faster than light (that
  :2548: 
  :2549: only covers about 200 miles in a millisecond), there is no way for the provers to communicate and
  :2550: 
  :2551: coordinate their answers, no matter what is inside the box.
  :2552: 
  :2553: The upshot is that if someone provides you with such devices that consistently succeed in this
  :2554: 
  :2555: experiment with more than 3/4 = 0.75 probability, then she has refuted Einstein's theory. As we
  :2556: 
  :2557: will see later in Section 20.3.2, quantum mechanics, with its instantaneous effects of measurements,
  :2558: 
  :2559: can be used to actually build devices that succeed in this game with probability at least 0.8 (there
  :2560: 
  :2561: are other games with more dramatic differences of probabilities) and this has been experimentally
  :2562: 
  :2563: DRAFT demonstrated.                                          Web draft 2007-01-08 21:59
  :2564: 
  :2565: 20.2. A NEW VIEW OF PROBABILISTIC COMPUTATION.  p20.5 (405)
  :2566: 
  :2567: 20.2 A new view of probabilistic computation.
  :2568: 
  :2569: To understand quantum computation, it is helpful to first take a different viewpoint of a process
  :2570: 
  :2571: we are already familiar with: probabilistic computation.
  :2572: 
  :2573: Suppose that we have an m-bit register. Normally, we think of such a register as having
  :2574: some definite value x  {0, 1}m. However, in the context of probabilistic computation, we can
  :2575: 
  :2576: also think of the register's state as actually being a probability distribution over its possible val-
  :2577: ues. That is, we think of the register's state as being described by a 2m-dimensional vector
  :2578: v = v0m, v0m-11, . . . , v1m , where for every x  {0, 1}m, vx  [0, 1] and x vx = 1. When
  :2579: we read, or measure, the register, we will obtain the value x with probability vx.
  :2580: 
  :2581: For every x  {0, 1}n, we denote by |x the vector that corresponds to the degenerate distribu-
  :2582: tion that takes the value x with probability 1. That is, |x is the 2m-dimensional vector that has
  :2583: zeroes in all the coordinates except a single 1 in the xth coordinate. Note that v = x{0,1}m vx |x .
  :2584: (We think of all these vectors as column vectors in the space Rm.)
  :2585: 
  :2586: Example 20.3
  :2587: If a 1-bit register's state is the distribution that takes the value 0 with probability p and 1 with
  :2588: probability 1 - p, then we describe the state as the vector p |0 + (1 - p) |1 .
  :2589: 
  :2590: The uniform distribution over the possible values of a 2-bit register is represented by 1/4 (|00 + |01 + |10 + |11
  :2591: The distribution that is uniform on every individual bit, but always satisfies that the two bits are
  :2592: equal is represented by 1/2 (|00 + |11 ).
  :2593: 
  :2594: An probabilistic operation on the register involves reading its value, and, based on the value
  :2595: read, modifying it in some deterministic or probabilistic way. If F is some probabilistic operation,
  :2596: then we can think of F as a function from R2m to R2m that maps the previous state of the register
  :2597: to its new state after the operation is performed. There are certain properties that every such
  :2598: operation must satisfy:
  :2599: 
  :2600: � Since F depends only on the contents of the register, and not on the overall distribution, for
  :2601: every v, F (v) = x{0,1}m vxF (|v ). That is, F is a linear function. (Note that this means
  :2602: that F can be described by a 2n � 2n matrix.)
  :2603: 
  :2604: � If v is a distribution vector (i.e., a vector of non-negative entries that sum up to one), then so
  :2605: is F (v). That is, F is a stochastic function. (Note that this means that viewed as a matrix,
  :2606: F has non-negative entries with each column summing up to 1.)
  :2607: 
  :2608: Example 20.4
  :2609: The operation that, regardless of the register's value, writes into it a uniformly chosen random
  :2610: string, is described by the function F such that F (|x ) = 2-m x{0,1}m |x for every x  {0, 1}m.
  :2611: (Because the set {|x }x{0,1}n is a basis for R2m, a linear function is completely determined by its
  :2612: 
  :2613: DRAFT output on these vectors.)
  :2614: Web draft 2007-01-08 21:59
  :2615: 
  :2616: p20.6 (406)                                                      20.2. A NEW VIEW OF PROBABILISTIC COMPUTATION.
  :2617: 
  :2618: The operation that flips the first bit of the register is described by the function F such that
  :2619: F (|x1 . . . xm ) = |(1 - x1)x2 . . . xm for every x1, . . . , xm  {0, 1}.
  :2620: 
  :2621: Of course there are many probabilistic operations that cannot be efficiently computed, but there
  :2622: 
  :2623: are very simple operations that can certainly be computed. An operation F is elementary if it only
  :2624: 
  :2625: reads and modifies at most three bits of the register, leaving the rest of the register untouched.
  :2626: That is, there is some operation G : R23  R23 and three indices j, k,  [m] such that for every
  :2627: x1, . . . , xm  {0, 1}, F (|x1 . . . xm ) = |y1 . . . ym where |yjyky = G(|xjxkx ) and yi = xi for
  :2628: every i  {j, k, }. Note that such an operation can be represented by a 23 � 23 matrix and three
  :2629: 
  :2630: indices in [m].

  :2656: previous definition of probabilistic computation as in the class BPP defined in Chapter 7.

  :2658: Definition 20.6 (Probabilistic Computation)
  :2659: Let f : {0, 1}  {0, 1} and T : N  N be some functions. We say that f is computable in
  :2660: probabilistic T (n)-time if for every n  N and x  {0, 1}n, f (x) can be computed by the following
  :2661:

  :2665:

  :2667: require that there is a polynomial-time TM that on input 1n, 1T (n) outputs the descriptions
  :2668: 
  :2669: of F1, . . . , FT ).
  :2670: 
  :2671: 3. Measure the register and let Y denote the obtained value. (That is, if v is the final state of
  :2672: 
  :2673: the register, then Y is a random variable that takes the value y with probability vy for every
  :2674: DRAFT y  {0, 1}n.)

  :2678: 
  :2679: Denoting = |f (x)|, we require that the first bits of Y are equal to f (x) with probability at
  :2680: least 2/3.
  :2681: 
  :2682: Probabilistic computation: summary of notations.
  :2683: The state of an m-bit register is represented by a vector v  R2m such that
  :2684: the register takes the value x with probability vx.
  :2685: An operation on the register is a function F : R2m  R2m that is linear and
  :2686: stochastic.
  :2687: An elementary operation only reads and modifies at most three bits of the
  :2688: register.
  :2689: A computation of a function f on input x  {0, 1}n involves initializing the
  :2690: register to the state |x0m-n , applying a sequence of elementary operations
  :2691: to it, and then measuring its value.

  :2693: the one encountered in Chapter 7.

  :2785: 20.3 Quantum superposition and the class BQP
  :2786: 
  :2787: A quantum register is also composed of m bits, but in quantum parlance they are called "qubits".
  :2788: In principle such a register can be implemented by any collection of m physical systems that can
  :2789: have an ON and OFF states, although in practice there are significant challenges for such an
  :2790: implementation (see Note 20.1). According to quantum mechanics, the state of such a register can
  :2791: be described by a 2m-dimensional vector that, unlike the probabilistic case, can actually contain
  :2792: negative and even complex numbers. That is, the state of the register is described by a vector
  :2793: v  C2m. Once again, we denote v = x{0,1}n vx |x (where again |x is the column vector that
  :2794: 
  :2795: DRAFT has all zeroes and a single one in the xth coordinate). However, according to quantum mechanics,
  :2796: Web draft 2007-01-08 21:59
  :2797: 
  :2798: 20.3. QUANTUM SUPERPOSITION AND THE CLASS BQP                                                     p20.9 (409)
  :2799: 
  :2800: when the register is measured, the probability that we see the value x is given not by vx but by
  :2801: |vx|2. This means that v has to be a unit vector, satisfying x |vx|2 = 1 (see Note 20.8).
  :2802: 
  :2803: Example 20.9
  :2804:

  :2809: 2           2

  :2812: 
  :2813: differentiate between them using quantum operations.
  :2814:

  :2816: 
  :2817: |0 - |1 to denote the state 1 |0 - 1 |1 .

  :2984: 
  :2985: Quantum computation: summary of notations.
  :2986: The state of an m-qubit register is represented by a unit vector v  C2m
  :2987: such that the register takes the value x with probability |vx|2.
  :2988: An operation on the register is a function F : C2m  C2m that is unitary.
  :2989: (i.e., linear and norm preserving).
  :2990: An elementary operation only depends and modifies at most three bits of
  :2991: the register.
  :2992: A computation of a function f on input x  {0, 1}n involves initializing the
  :2993: register to the state |x0m-n , applying a sequence of elementary operations
  :2994: to it, and then measuring its value.
  :2995: 
  :2996: Remark 20.15
  :2997: Readers familiar with quantum mechanics or quantum computing may notice that we did not allow
  :2998: in our definition of quantum computation several features that are allowed by quantum mechanics.
  :2999: These include mixed states, that involve both quantum superposition and probability, measuring
  :3000: in different basis than the standard basis, and performing partial measurements during the com-
  :3001: putation. However, none of these features adds to the computing power of quantum computers.
  :3002: 
  :3003: 20.3.1 Universal quantum operations
  :3004: 
  :3005: Can we actually implement quantum computation? This is an excellent question, and no one really
  :3006: knows. However, one hurdle can be overcome: even though there is an infinite set of possible
  :3007: elementary operations, all of them can be generated (or at least sufficiently well approximated) by
  :3008: the Hadamard and Tofolli operations described in Example 20.12. In fact, every operation that
  :3009: depends on k qubits can be approximated by composing 2O(k) of these four operations (times an
  :3010: additional small factor depending on the approximation's quality). Using a counting/dimension
  :3011: argument, it can be shown that some unitary transformations do indeed require an exponential
  :3012: number of elementary operations to compute (or even approximate).
  :3013: 
  :3014: One useful consequence of universality is the following: when designing quantum algorithms we
  :3015: can assume that we have at our disposal the all operations that depend on k qubits as elementary
  :3016: operations, for every constant k (even if k > 3). This is since these can be implemented by 3 qubit
  :3017: elementary operations incurring only a constant (depending on k) overhead.
  :3018: 
  :3019: 20.3.2 Spooky coordination and Bell's state
  :3020: 
  :3021: To get our first glimpse of how things behave differently in the quantum world, we will now show
  :3022: how quantum registers and operations help us win the game described in Section 20.1.2 with higher
  :3023: probability than can be achieved according to pre-quantum "classical" physics.
  :3024: Recall that the game was the following:
  :3025: 
  :3026: 1. The verifier chooses random x, y R {0, 1} and sends x to Alice and y to Bob, collecting their
  :3027: respective answers a and b.
  :3028: 
  :3029: 2. It accepts iff x  y = a  b. In other words, it accepts if either x, y = 1, 1 and a = b or
  :3030: 
  :3031: DRAFT x=y =1 and a=b.
  :3032: Web draft 2007-01-08 21:59
  :3033: 
  :3034: p20.14 (414)                  20.3. QUANTUM SUPERPOSITION AND THE CLASS BQP
  :3035: 
  :3036: It was shown in Section 20.1.2 that if Alice and Bob can not coordinate their actions then the
  :3037: verifier will accept with probability at most 3/4, but quantum effects can allow them to bypass this
  :3038: bound as follows:
  :3039: 
  :3040: 1. Alice and Bob prepare a 2-qubit quantum register containing the EPR state |00 + |11 .
  :3041: (They can start with a register initialized to |00 and then apply an elementary operation
  :3042: that maps the initial state to the EPR state.)
  :3043: 
  :3044: 2. Alice and Bob split the register - Alice takes the first qubit and Bob takes the second qubit.
  :3045: (The components containing each qubit of a quantum register do not necessarily need to be
  :3046: adjacent to one another.)
  :3047: 
  :3048: 3. Alice receives the qubit x from the verifier, and if x = 1 then she applies a rotation by /8
  :3049: (22.5�) operation to her qubit. (Since the operation involves only her qubit, she can perform
  :3050: it even after the register was split.)
  :3051: 
  :3052: 4. Bob receives the qubit y from the verifier, and if y = 1 he applies a rotation by by -/8
  :3053: (-22.5�) operation to his qubit.
  :3054: 
  :3055: 5. Both of them measure their respective qubits and output the values obtained as their answers
  :3056: a and b.
  :3057: 
  :3058: Note that the order in which Alice and Bob perform their rotations and measurements does not
  :3059: matter - it can be shown that all orders yield exactly the same distribution (e.g., see Exercise 3).
  :3060: While splitting a quantum register and applying unitary transformations to the different parts
  :3061: may sound far fetched, this experiment had been performed several times in practice, verifying the
  :3062: following predictions of quantum mechanics:
  :3063: 
  :3064: Theorem 20.16
  :3065: Given the above strategy for Alice and Bob, the verifier will accept with probability at least 0.8.
  :3066: 
  :3067: Proof: Recall that Alice and Bob win the game if they output the same answer when x, y =
  :3068: 1, 1 and a different answer otherwise. The intuition behind the proof is that in the case that
  :3069: x, y = 1, 1 then the states of the two qubits will be "close" to one another (the angle between
  :3070: them is less than /8 or 22.5�) and in the other case the states will be "far" (having angle /4 or
  :3071: 45�). Specifically we will show that:
  :3072: 
  :3073: (1) If x = y = 0 then a = b with probability 1.
  :3074: 
  :3075: (2) If x = y then a = b with probability cos2(/8)  0.85
  :3076: 
  :3077: (3) If x = y = 1 then a = b with probability 1/2.
  :3078: 
  :3079: Implying  that  the  overall  acceptance  probability  is  at  least  1  +  1  0.85  +  1  =  0.8.
  :3080: 4     2           8
  :3081: 
  :3082: In the case (1) both Alice and Bob perform no operation on their register, and so when measured
  :3083: 
  :3084: it will be either in the state |00 or |11 , both resulting in Alice and Bob's outputs being equal. To
  :3085: 
  :3086: DRAFT analyze case (2), it suffices to consider the case that x = 0, y = 1 (the other case is symmetrical).
  :3087: Web draft 2007-01-08 21:59
  :3088: 
  :3089: 20.4. QUANTUM PROGRAMMER'S TOOLKIT  p20.15 (415)
  :3090: 
  :3091: In this case Alice applies no transformation to her qubit, and Bob rotates his qubit in a -/8 angle.
  :3092: Imagine that Bob first makes the rotation, then Alice measures her qubit and then Bob measures
  :3093: his (this is OK as the order of measurements does not change the outcome). With probability 1/2,
  :3094: Alice will get the value 0 and Bob's qubit will collapse to the state |0 rotated by a -/8 angle,
  :3095: meaning that when measuring Bob will obtain the value 0 with probability cos2(/8). Similarly, if
  :3096: Alice gets the value 1 then Bob will also output 1 with cos2(/8) probability.
  :3097: 
  :3098: To analyze case (3), we just use direct computation. In this case, after both rotations are
  :3099: performed, the register's state is
  :3100: 
  :3101: (cos(/8) |0 + sin(/8) |1 ) (cos(/8) |0 - sin(/8) |1 ) +
  :3102: (- sin(/8) |0 + cos(/8) |1 ) (sin(/8) |0 + cos(/8) |1 ) =
  :3103: cos2(/8) - sin2(/8) |00 - 2 sin(/8) cos(/8) |01 +
  :3104: 2 sin(/8) cos(/8) |10 + cos2(/8) - sin2(/8) |11 .
  :3105: 
  :3106: But since
  :3107: 
  :3108: cos2(/8) - sin2(/8) = cos(/4) = 1 = sin(/4) = 2 sin(/8) cos(/8) ,
  :3109: 
  :3110: 2
  :3111: 
  :3112: all coefficients in this state have the same absolute value and hence when measured the register
  :3113: will yield either one of the four values 00, 01, 10 and 11 with equal probability 1/4.
  :3114: 
  :3115: 20.4 Quantum programmer's toolkit
  :3116: 
  :3117: Quantum algorithms have some peculiar features that classical algorithm designers are not used to.
  :3118: The following observations can serve as a helpful "bag of tricks" for designing quantum algorithms:
  :3119: 
  :3120: � If we can compute an n-qubit unitary transformation U in T steps then we can compute the
  :3121: transformation Controlled-U in O(T ) steps, where Controlled-U maps a vector |x1 . . . xnxn+1
  :3122: to |U (x1 . . . xn)xn+1 if xn+1 = 1 and to itself otherwise.
  :3123: The reason is that we can transform every elementary operation F in the computation of U
  :3124: to the analogous "Controlled-F " operation. Since the "Controlled-F " operation depends on
  :3125: at most 4 qubits, it can be considered also as elementary.
  :3126: 
  :3127: For every two n-qubit transformations U, U , we can use this observation twice to compute
  :3128: the transformation that invokes U on x1 . . . xn if xn+1 = 1 and invokes U otherwise.
  :3129: 
  :3130: � Every permutation of the standard basis is unitary. That is, any operation that maps a vector
  :3131: |x into |(x) where  is a permutation of {0, 1}n is unitary. Of course, this does not mean
  :3132: that all such permutations are efficiently computable in quantum polynomial time.
  :3133: 
  :3134: � For every function f : {0, 1}n  {0, 1} , the function x, y  x, (y  f (x)) is a permutation
  :3135: on {0, 1}n+ (in fact, this function is its own inverse). In particular, this means that we
  :3136: 
  :3137: DRAFT can use as elementary operations the following "permutation variants" of AND, OR and
  :3138: Web draft 2007-01-08 21:59
  :3139: 
  :3140: p20.16 (416)                                  20.5. GROVER'S SEARCH ALGORITHM.
  :3141: 
  :3142: copying: (1) |x1x2x3  |x1x2(x3  (x1 x2)) , (2) |x1x2x3  |x1x2(x3  (x1 x2)) , and
  :3143: (3) |x1x2  |x1(x1  x2) . Note that in all these cases we compute the "right" function if
  :3144: the last qubit is initially equal to 0.
  :3145: 
  :3146: � If f : {0, 1}n  {0, 1} is a function computable by a size-T Boolean circuit, then the
  :3147: following transformation can be computed by a sequence of O(T ) elementary operations: for
  :3148: every x  {0, 1}m , y  {0, 1} , z  {0, 1}T
  :3149: 
  :3150: |x, y, z  x, (y  f (x)), 0T if z = 0T .
  :3151: 
  :3152: (We don't care on what the mapping does for z = 0T .)
  :3153: 
  :3154: The reason is that by transforming every AND, OR or NOT gate into the corresponding
  :3155: elementary permutation we can ensure that the ith qubit of z contains the result of the ith
  :3156: gate of the circuit when executed on input x. We can then XOR the result of the circuit into
  :3157: y using elementary operations and run the entire computation backward to return the state
  :3158: of z to 0T . .
  :3159: 
  :3160: � We can assume that we are allowed to make a partial measurement in the course of the
  :3161: 
  :3162: algorithm, and then proceed differently according to its outcome. That is, we can measure a
  :3163: 
  :3164: some of the qubits of the register. Note that if the register is at state v and we measure its ith
  :3165: 
  :3166: qubit then with probability z:zi=1 |vz|2 we will get the answer "1" and the register's state
  :3167: 
  :3168: will change   to (the normalized version      of) the vector                   z:zi=1 vz |z . Symmetrically, with
  :3169: probability     z:zi=0 |vz|2 we will get the  answer "0" and                 the new state will be z:zi=0 vz |z .
  :3170: 
  :3171: This is allowed since an algorithm using partial measurement can be replaced with an algo-
  :3172: 
  :3173: rithm not using it with at most a constant overhead (see Exercise 4).
  :3174: 
  :3175: � Since the 1-qubit Hadamard operation maps |0 to the uniform state |0 + |1 , it can be used
  :3176: to simulate tossing a coin: we simply take a qubit in our workspace that is initialized to 0,
  :3177: apply Hadamard to it, and measure the result.
  :3178: 
  :3179: Together, the last three observations imply that quantum computation is at least as powerful
  :3180: as "classical" non-quantum computation:
  :3181: 
  :3182: Theorem 20.17
  :3183: BPP  BQP.

  :3185: 20.5 Grover's search algorithm.
  :3186: 
  :3187: Consider the NP-complete problem SAT of finding, given an n-variable Boolean formula , whether
  :3188: there exists an assignment a  {0, 1}n such that (a) = 1. Using "classical" deterministic or
  :3189: probabilistic TM's, we do not know how to solve this problem better than the trivial poly(n)2n-time
  :3190: algorithm.2 We now show a beautiful algorithm due to Grover that solves SAT in poly(n)2n/2-time
  :3191: 
  :3192: on a quantum computer. This is a significant improvement over the classical case, even if it falls
  :3193:

  :3371: 
  :3372: 20.6 Simon's Algorithm
  :3373: 
  :3374: Although beautiful, Grover's algorithm still has a significant drawback: it is merely quadratically
  :3375: faster than the best known classical algorithm for the same problem. In contrast, in this section we
  :3376: show Simon's algorithm that is a polynomial-time quantum algorithm solving a problem for which
  :3377: the best known classical algorithm takes exponential time.
  :3378: 
  :3379: Simon's algorithm solves the following problem: given a polynomial-time computable function
  :3380: f : {0, 1}n  {0, 1}n such that there exists a  {0, 1} satisfying f (x) = f (y) iff x = y  a for every
  :3381: x, y  {0, 1}n, find this string a.
  :3382: 
  :3383: Two natural questions are (1) why is this problem interesting? and (2) why do we believe it is
  :3384: hard to solve for classical computers? The best answer to (1) is that, as we will see in Section 20.7, a
  :3385: generalization of Simon's problem turns out to be crucial in the quantum polynomial-time algorithm
  :3386: for famous integer factorization problem. Regarding (2), of course we do not know for certain that
  :3387: this problem does not have a classical polynomial-time algorithm (in particular, if P = NP then
  :3388: there obviously exists such an algorithm). However, some intuition why it may be hard can be
  :3389: gleaned from the following black box model: suppose that you are given access to a black box (or
  :3390: oracle) that on input x  {0, 1}n, returns the value f (x). Would you be able to learn a by making
  :3391: at most a subexponential number of queries to the black box? It is not hard to see that if a is chosen
  :3392: at random from {0, 1}n and f is chosen at random subject to the condition that f (x) = f (y) iff
  :3393: x = ya then no algorithm can successfully recover a with reasonable probability using significantly
  :3394: less than 2n/2 queries to the black box. Indeed, an algorithm using fewer queries is very likely to
  :3395: never get the same answer to two distinct queries, in which case it gets no information about the
  :3396: value of a.
  :3397: 
  :3398: 20.6.1 The algorithm
  :3399: 
  :3400: Simon's algorithm is actually quite simple. It uses a register of 2n + m qubits, where m is the
  :3401: 
  :3402: number of workspace bits needed to compute f . (Below we will ignore the last m qubits of the
  :3403: 
  :3404: register, since they will be always set to all zeroes except in intermediate steps of f 's computation.)
  :3405: 
  :3406: The algorithm first uses n Hadamard operations to set the first n qubits to the uniform state and
  :3407: 
  :3408: then apply the operation |xz  |x(z  f (x) to the register, resulting (up to normalization) in
  :3409: 
  :3410: the state
  :3411: 
  :3412: |x |f (x) =           (|x + |x  a ) |f (x) .          (1)
  :3413: 
  :3414: x{0,1}n                 x{0,1}n
  :3415: 
  :3416: We then measure the second n bits of the register, collapsing its state to
  :3417: 
  :3418: |xf (x) + |(x  a)f (x)                             (2)
  :3419: 
  :3420: for some string x (that is chosen uniformly from {0, 1}n). You might think that we're done as the
  :3421: state (2) clearly encodes a, however we cannot directly learn a from this state: if we measure the
  :3422: first n bits we will get with probability 1/2 the value x and with probability 1/2 the value xa. Even
  :3423: though a can be deduced from these two values combined, each one of them on its own yields no
  :3424: 
  :3425: DRAFT information about a. (This point is well worth some contemplation, as it underlies the subtleties
  :3426: Web draft 2007-01-08 21:59
  :3427: 
  :3428: 20.7. SHOR'S ALGORITHM: INTEGER FACTORIZATION USING QUANTUM
  :3429: 
  :3430: p20.22 (422)                                                     COMPUTERS.
  :3431: 
  :3432: involved in quantum computation and demonstrates why a quantum algorithm is not generally
  :3433: equivalent to performing exponentially many classical computation in parallel.)
  :3434: 
  :3435: However, consider now what happens if we perform another n Hadamard operations on the first
  :3436: n bits. Since this maps x to the vector y(-1)x y |y , the new state of the first n bits will be
  :3437: 
  :3438: (-1)x y + (-1)(xa) y |y =      (-1)x y + (-1)x y(-1)a y |y .                   (3)
  :3439: 
  :3440: y                              y
  :3441: 
  :3442: For every y  {0, 1}m, the yth coefficient in the state (3) is nonzero if and only if if and only if
  :3443: a y = 0, and in fact if measured, the state (3) yields a uniform y  {0, 1}n satisfying a y = 0.
  :3444: 
  :3445: Repeating the entire process k times, we get k uniform strings y1, . . . , yk satisfying y a = 0
  :3446: or in other words, k linear equations (over the field GF(2)) on the variables a1, . . . , an. It can be
  :3447: easily shown that if, say, k  2n then with high probability there will be n - 1 linearly independent
  :3448: equations among these (see Exercise 5), and hence we will be able to retrieve a from these equations
  :3449: using Gaussian elimination. For completeness, a full description of Simon's algorithm can be found
  :3450: in Figure 20.4.

  :3454: a  {0, 1}n satisfying f (x) = f (y) iff y = x  a for every x, y  {0, 1}n, find a.
  :3455:

  :3477: Figure 20.4: Simon's Algorithm
  :3478: 
  :3479: 20.7 Shor's algorithm: integer factorization using quantum com-
  :3480: puters.
  :3481: 
  :3482: The integer factorization problem is to find, given an integer N , the set of all prime factors of N
  :3483: 
  :3484: DRAFT (i.e., prime numbers that divide N). By a polynomial-time algorithm for this problem we mean an
  :3485: Web draft 2007-01-08 21:59
  :3486: 
  :3487: 20.7. SHOR'S ALGORITHM: INTEGER FACTORIZATION USING QUANTUM
  :3488: 
  :3489: COMPUTERS.                                                   p20.23 (423)
  :3490: 
  :3491: algorithm that runs in time polynomial in the description of N , i.e., poly(log(N )) time. Although
  :3492: people have been thinking about the factorization problem in one form or another for at least 2000
  :3493: years, we still do not know of a polynomial-time algorithm for it: the best classical algorithm takes
  :3494: roughly 2(log N)1/3 steps to factor N [?]. In fact, the presumed difficulty of this problem underlies
  :3495: many popular encryption schemes (such as RSA). Therefore, it was quite a surprise when in 1994
  :3496: Peter Shor showed a quantum polynomial-time algorithm for this problem. To this day it remains
  :3497: the most famous algorithm for quantum computers, and the strongest evidence that BQP may
  :3498: contain problems outside of BPP.
  :3499: 
  :3500: The order-finding problem. Rather than showing an algorithm to factor a given number N ,
  :3501: we will show an algorithm for a related problem: given a number A with gcd(A, N ) = 1, find the
  :3502: order of A modulo N , defined to be the smallest positive integer r such that Ar = 1 (mod N ).
  :3503: Using elementary number theory, it is fairly straightforward to reduce the task of factoring N to
  :3504: solving this problem, and we defer the description of this reduction to Section 20.7.3.
  :3505: 
  :3506: Remark 20.18
  :3507: It is easy to see that for every positive integer k, if Ak = 1 (mod N ) then r divides k. (Indeed,
  :3508: otherwise if k = cr + d for c  Z and d  {1, .., r - 1} then Ad = 1 (mod N ), contradicting the
  :3509: minimality of r.) Similarly, for every x, y it holds that Ax = Ay (mod N ) iff x - y is a multiple of
  :3510: r. Therefore, the order finding problem can be defined as follows: given the function f : N  N
  :3511: that maps x to Ax (mod N ) and satisfies that f (x) = f (y) iff r|x - y, find r. In this notation, the
  :3512: similarity to Simon's problem becomes more apparent.
  :3513: 
  :3514: 20.7.1 Quantum Fourier Transform over ZM .
  :3515: 
  :3516: The main tool used to solve the order-finding problem is the quantum Fourier transform. We have
  :3517: 
  :3518: already encountered the Fourier transform in Chapter 19, but will now use a different variant, which
  :3519: we call the Fourier transform over ZM where M = 2m for some integer M . Recall that ZM is the
  :3520: group of all number in {0, . . . , M - 1} with the group operation being addition modulo M . The
  :3521: Fourier transform over this group, defined below, is a linear and in fact unitary operation from C2m
  :3522: to C2m. The quantum Fourier transform is a way to perform this operation by composing O(m2)
  :3523: elementary quantum operations (operations that depend on at most three qubits). This means that
  :3524: 
  :3525: we can transform a quantum system whose register is in state f to a system whose register is in the
  :3526: state corresponding to the Fourier transform f^ of f . This does not mean that we can compute in
  :3527: O(m2) the Fourier transform over ZM - indeed this is not sufficient time to even write the output!
  :3528: Nonetheless, this transformation still turns out to be very useful, and is crucial to Shor's factoring
  :3529: 
  :3530: algorithm in the same way that the Hadamard transformation (which is a Fourier transform over
  :3531: the group {0, 1}n with the operation ) was crucial to Simon's algorithm.
  :3532: 
  :3533: Definition of the Fourier transform over ZM .

  :3832: 20.7.3 Reducing factoring to order finding.
  :3833: 
  :3834: The reduction of the factoring problem to the order-finding problem follows immediately from the
  :3835: following two Lemmas:
  :3836: 
  :3837: Lemma 20.23
  :3838: For every nonprime N , the probability that a random X in the set ZN = {X  [N - 1] : gcd(X, N ) = 1}
  :3839: has an even order r and furthermore, Xr/2 = +1 (mod N ) and X = -1 (mod N ) is at least 1/4.
  :3840: 
  :3841: Lemma 20.24
  :3842: For every N and Y , if Y 2 = 1 (mod N ) but Y = +1 (mod N ) and Y = -1 (mod N ), then
  :3843: gcd(Y - 1, N ) > 1.
  :3844: 
  :3845: Together, Lemmas 20.23 and 20.24 show that the following algorithm will output a prime factor
  :3846: P of N with high probability: (once we have a single prime factor P , we can run the algorithm
  :3847: again on N/P )
  :3848: 
  :3849: 1. Choose X at random from [N - 1].
  :3850: 
  :3851: 2. If gcd(X, N ) > 1 then let K = gcd(X, N ), otherwise compute the order r of X, and if r is
  :3852: even let K = gcd(Xr/2 - 1, N ).
  :3853: 
  :3854: 3. If K  {1, N } then go back to Step 1. If K is a prime then output K and halt. Otherwise,
  :3855: use recursion to output a factor of K.
  :3856: 
  :3857: Note that if T (N ) is the running time of the algorithm then it satisfies the equation T (N )
  :3858: T (N/2) + polylog(N ) leading to polylog(N ) running time.
  :3859: Proof of Lemma 20.24: Under our assumptions, N divides Y 2 - 1 = (Y - 1)(X + 1) but does
  :3860: not divide neither Y - 1 or Y + 1. But this means that gcd(Y - 1, N ) > 1Z since if Y - 1 and N
  :3861: were coprime, then since N divides (Y - 1)(Y + 1), it would have to divide X + 1 (Exercise 8).
  :3862: 
  :3863: Proof of Lemma 20.23: We prove this for the case that N = P Q for two primes P, Q (the proof
  :3864: for the general case is similar and is left as Exercise ??). In this case, by the Chinese Reminder
  :3865: Theorem, if we map every number X  ZN to the pair X (mod P ), X (mod Q) then this map
  :3866: is one-to-one. Also, the groups ZP and ZQ are known to by cyclic which means that there is a
  :3867: number g  [P - 1] such that the map j  gj (mod P ) is a permutation of [P - 1] and similarly
  :3868: there is a number h  [Q - 1] such that the map k  hk (mod P ) is a permutation of [Q - 1].
  :3869: 
  :3870: This means that instead of choosing X at random, we can think of choosing two numbers j, k at
  :3871: random from [P -1] and [Q-1] respectively and consider the pair gj (mod P ), hk (mod Q) which
  :3872: is in one-to-one correspondence with the set of X's in ZN . The order of this pair (or equivalently,
  :3873: 
  :3874: DRAFT of X) is the smallest positive integer r such that gjr = 1 (mod P) and hkr = 1 (mod Q), which
  :3875: Web draft 2007-01-08 21:59
  :3876: 
  :3877: 20.8. BQP AND CLASSICAL COMPLEXITY CLASSES  p20.29 (429)
  :3878: 
  :3879: means that P - 1|jr and Q - 1|kr. Now suppose that j is odd and k is even (this happens with
  :3880: 
  :3881: probability 1/4). In this case r is of the form 2r where r is the smallest number such that P -1|2jr
  :3882: 
  :3883: and Q - 1|kr (the latter holds since we can divide the two even numbers k and Q - 1 by two). But
  :3884: this means that gj(r/2) = 1 (mod Q) and hk(r/2) = 1 (mod Q). In other words, if we let X be the
  :3885: number corresponding to gj (mod P ), hk (mod Q) then Xr/2 corresponds to a pair of the form
  :3886: 
  :3887: a, 1 where a = 1. However, since +1 (mod N ) corresponds to the pair +1, +1 and -1 (mod N )
  :3888: corresponds to the pair -1 (mod P ), -1 (mod Q) it follows that Xr/2 = �1 (mod N ).
  :3889: 
  :3890: 20.8 BQP and classical complexity classes
  :3891: 
  :3892: What is the relation between BQP and the classes we already encountered such as P, BPP and
  :3893: NP? This is very much an open questions. It not hard to show that quantum computers are at
  :3894: least not infinitely powerful compared to classical algorithms:
  :3895: 
  :3896: Theorem 20.25
  :3897: BQP  PSPACE
  :3898: 
  :3899: Proof Sketch: To simulate a T -step quantum computation on an m bit register, we need to
  :3900: come up with a procedure Coeff that for every i  [T ] and x  {0, 1}m, the xth coefficient (up to
  :3901: some accuracy) of the register's state in the ith execution. We can compute Coeff on inputs x, i
  :3902: using at most 8 recursive calls to Coeff on inputs x , i - 1 (for the at most 8 strings that agree
  :3903: with x on the three bits that the Fi's operation reads and modifies). Since we can reuse the space
  :3904: used by the recursive operations, if we let S(i) denote the space needed to compute Coeff(x, i)
  :3905: then S(i)  S(i - 1) + O( ) (where is the number of bits used to store each coefficient).
  :3906: 
  :3907: To compute, say, the probability that if measured after the final step the first bit of the register
  :3908: is equal to 1, just compute the sum of Coeff(x, T ) for every x  {0, 1}n. Again, by reusing the
  :3909: space of each computation this can be done using polynomial space.
  :3910: 
  :3911: Theorem 20.25 can be improved to show that BQP  P#P (where #P is the counting version
  :3912: of NP described in Chapter 9), but this is currently the best upper bound we know on BQP.
  :3913: 
  :3914: Does BQP = BPP? The main reason to believe this is false is the polynomial-time algorithm
  :3915: for integer factorization. Although this is not as strong as the evidence for, say NP BPP
  :3916: (after all NP contains thousands of well-studied problems that have resisted efficient algorithms),
  :3917: the factorization problem is one of the oldest and most well-studied computational problems, and
  :3918: the fact that we still know no efficient algorithm for it makes the conjecture that none exists
  :3919: appealing. Also note that unlike other famous problems that eventually found an algorithm (e.g.,
  :3920: linear programming [?] and primality testing [?]), we do not even have a heuristic algorithm that
  :3921: is conjectured to work (even without proof) or experimentally works on, say, numbers that are
  :3922: product of two random large primes.
  :3923: 
  :3924: What is the relation between BQP and NP? It seems that quantum computers only offer
  :3925: a quadratic speedup (using Grover's search) on NP-complete problems, and so most researchers
  :3926: believe that NP BPP. On the other hand, there is a problem in BQP (the Recursive Fourier
  :3927: Sampling or RFS problem [BV97]) that is not known to be in the polynomial-hierarchy , and so at
  :3928: the moment we do not know that BQP = BPP even if we were given a polynomial-time algorithm
  :3929: 
  :3930: DRAFT for SAT.
  :3931: Web draft 2007-01-08 21:59
  :3932: 
  :3933: p20.30 (430)  20.8. BQP AND CLASSICAL COMPLEXITY CLASSES
  :3934: 
  :3935: Chapter notes and history
  :3936: 
  :3937: We did not include treatment of many fascinating aspects of quantum information and computation.
  :3938: Many of these are covered in the book by Nielsen and Chuang [NC00]. See also Umesh Vazirani's
  :3939: excellent lecture notes on the topic (available from his home page).
  :3940: 
  :3941: One such area is quantum error correction, that tackles the following important issue: how can
  :3942: we run a quantum algorithm when at every possible step there is a probability of noise interfering
  :3943: with the computation? It turns out that under reasonable noise models, one can prove the following
  :3944: threshold theorem: as long as the probability of noise at a single step is lower than some constant
  :3945: threshold, one can perform arbitrarily long computations and get the correct answer with high
  :3946: probability [?].
  :3947: 
  :3948: Quantum computing has a complicated but interesting relation to cryptography. Although
  :3949: Shor's algorithm and its variants break many of the well known public key cryptosystems (those
  :3950: based on the hardness of integer factorization and discrete log), the features of quantum mechanics
  :3951: can actually be used for cryptographic purposes, a research area called quantum cryptography (see
  :3952: [?]). Shor's algorithm also spurred research on basing public key encryption scheme on other
  :3953: computational problems (as far as we know, quantum computers do not make the task of breaking
  :3954: most known private key cryptosystems significantly easier). Perhaps the most promising direction
  :3955: is basing such schemes on certain problems on integer lattices (see the book [?] and [?]).
  :3956: 
  :3957: While quantum mechanics has had fantastic success in predicting experiments, some would
  :3958: require more from a physical theory. Namely, to tell us what is the "actual reality" of our world.
  :3959: Many physicists are understandably uncomfortable with the description of nature as maintaining
  :3960: a huge array of possible states, and changing its behavior when it is observed. The popular science
  :3961: book [Bru04] contains a good (even if a bit biased) review of physicists' and philosophers' attempts
  :3962: at providing more palatable descriptions that still manage to predict experiments.
  :3963: 
  :3964: On a more technical level, while no one doubts that quantum effects exist at microscopic scales,
  :3965: scientists questioned why they do not manifest themselves at the macrosopic level (or at least
  :3966: not to human consciousness). A Scientific American article by Yam [Yam97] describes various
  :3967: explanations that have been advanced over the years. The leading theory is decoherence, which
  :3968: tries to use quantum theory to explain the absence of macroscopic quantum effects. Researchers are
  :3969: not completely comfortable with this explanation. The issue is undoubtedly important to quantum
  :3970: computing, which requires hundreds of thousands of particles to stay in quantum superposition for
  :3971: large-ish periods of time. Thus far it is an open question whether this is practically achievable.
  :3972: One theoretical idea is to treat decoherence as a form of noise, and to build noise-tolerance into
  :3973: the computation --a nontrivial process. For details of this and many other topics, see the books
  :3974: by Kitaev, Shen, and Vyalyi [AA02].
  :3975: 
  :3976: The original motivation for quantum computing was to construct computers that are able to
  :3977: simulate quantum mechanical systems, and this still might be their most important application
  :3978: if they are ever built. Feynman [Fey82] was the first to suggest the possibility that quantum
  :3979: mechanics might allow Turing Machines more computational power than classical TMs. In 1985
  :3980: Deutsch [Deu85] defined a quantum Turing machine, though in retrospect his definition is unsatis-
  :3981: factory. Better definitions then appeared in Deutsch-Josza [DJ92], Bernstein-Vazirani [BV97] and
  :3982: 
  :3983: DRAFT Yao [Yao93], at which point quantum computation was firmly established as a field.
  :3984: Web draft 2007-01-08 21:59

  :4084: Chapter 21
  :4085: 
  :4086: Logic in complexity theory
  :4087: 
  :4088: Very sketchy
  :4089: 
  :4090: As mentioned in the book's introduction, complexity theory (indeed, all of computer science)
  :4091: 
  :4092: arose from developments in mathematical logic in the first half of the century. Mathematical logic
  :4093: 
  :4094: continues to exert an influence today, suggesting terminology and choice of problems (e.g., "boolean
  :4095: 
  :4096: satisfiability") as well as approaches for attacking complexity's central open questions. This chapter
  :4097: 
  :4098: is an introduction to the basic concepts.
  :4099: 
  :4100: Mathematical logic has also influenced many other areas of computer science, such as program-
  :4101: 
  :4102: ming languages, program verification, and model checking. We will not touch upon them, except
  :4103: 
  :4104: to note that they supply interesting examples of hard computational problems --ranging from
  :4105: 
  :4106: NP-complete to EXPSPACE-complete to undecidable.
  :4107: 
  :4108: The rest of the chapter assumes only a nodding familiarity with logic terminology, which we
  :4109: 
  :4110: now recount informally; for details see a logic text.
  :4111: 
  :4112: A logic usually refers to a set of rules about constructing valid sentences. Here are a few logics
  :4113: 
  :4114: we will encounter. Propositional logic concerns sentences such as (p  �q)  (�p  r) where p, q, r
  :4115: 
  :4116: are boolean variables. Recall that the SAT problem consists of determining the satisfiability of
  :4117: 
  :4118: such sentences. In first order logic, we allow relation and function symbols as well as quantification
  :4119: 
  :4120: symbols  and . For instance, the statement xS(x) = x is a first order sentence in which x is
  :4121: 
  :4122: quantified universally, S() is a unary relation symbol and = is a binary relation. Such logics are
  :4123: 
  :4124: used in well-known axiomatizations of mathematics, such as Euclidean geometry, Peano Arithmetic
  :4125: 
  :4126: or Zermelo Frankel set theory. Finally, second order logic allows sentences in which one is allowed
  :4127: 
  :4128: quantification over structures, i.e., functions and relations. An example of a second order sentence
  :4129: 
  :4130: is SxS(x) = x, where S is a unary relation symbol.
  :4131: 
  :4132: A sentence (or collection of sentences) in a logic has no intrinsic "meaning." The meaning
  :4133: 
  :4134: --including truth or falsehood--can be discussed only with reference to a structure, which gives
  :4135: 
  :4136: a way of interpreting all symbols in the sentence. To give an example, Peano arithmetic consists
  :4137: 
  :4138: of five sentences ("axioms") in a logic that consists of symbols like S(x), =, + etc. The standard
  :4139: 
  :4140: structure of these sentences is the set of positive integers, with S() given the intepretation of
  :4141: 
  :4142: "successor function," + given the interpretation of addition, and so on. A structure is said to be a
  :4143: 
  :4144: model for a sentence or a group of sentences if those sentences are true in that structure.
  :4145: 
  :4146: DRAFT Finally, a proof system consists of a set of sentences  called axioms and one or more derivation
  :4147: Web draft 2007-01-08 21:59                 p21.1 (433)
  :4148: 
  :4149: Complexity Theory: A Modern Approach. � 2006 Sanjeev Arora and Boaz Barak. References and attributions are
  :4150: 
  :4151: still incomplete.
  :4152: 
  :4153: p21.2 (434)  21.1. LOGICAL DEFINITIONS OF COMPLEXITY CLASSES
  :4154: 
  :4155: rules for deriving new sentences from the axioms. We say that sentence  can be proved from ,
  :4156: denoted  , if it can be derived from  using a finite number of applications of the derivation
  :4157: rules. A proveable sentence is called a theorem.
  :4158: 
  :4159: Note that a theorem is a result of a mechanical (essentially, algorithmic) process of applying
  :4160: derivation rules to the axioms. There is a related notion of whether or not  is logically implied by
  :4161: , denoted  |= , which means that every model of  is also a model of . In other words, there
  :4162: is no "counterexample model" in which the axioms  are true but  is not. The two notions are in
  :4163: general different but Go�del in his completeness theorem for first order theories exhibited a natural
  :4164: set of derivation rules such that logically implied sentences are exactly the set of theorems. (This
  :4165: result was a stepping stone to his even more famous incompleteness theorem.)
  :4166: 
  :4167: Later in this chapter we give a complexity-theoretic definition of a proof system, and introduce
  :4168: the area of proof complexity that studies the size of the smallest proof of a mathematical statement
  :4169: in a given proof system.
  :4170: 
  :4171: 21.1 Logical definitions of complexity classes
  :4172: 
  :4173: Just as Church and others defined computation using logic without referring to any kind of com-
  :4174: puting machine, it is possible to give "machineless" characterizations of many complexity classes
  :4175: using logic. We describe a few examples below.
  :4176: 
  :4177: 21.1.1 Fagin's definition of NP

  :4222: 21.1.2 MAX-SNP
  :4223: 
  :4224: 21.2 Proof complexity as an approach to NP versus coNP
  :4225: 
  :4226: Proof complexity tries to study the size of the smallest proof of a statement in a given proof
  :4227: system. First, we need a formal definition of what a proof system is. The following definition due
  :4228: to Cook and Reckow focuses attention on the intuitive property that a mathematical proof is "easy
  :4229: to check."
  :4230: 
  :4231: Definition 21.3
  :4232: A proof system consists of a polynomial-time Turing machine M . A statement T is said to be a
  :4233: theorem of this proof system iff there is a string   {0, 1} such that M accepts (T, ).
  :4234: 
  :4235: If T is a theorem of proof system M , then the proof complexity of T with respect to M is the
  :4236: minimun k such that there is some   {0, 1}k for which M accepts (T, ).
  :4237: 
  :4238: Note that the definition of theoremhood ignores the issue of the length of the proof, and insists
  :4239: only that the M 's running time is polynomial in the input length |T | + ||. The following is an
  :4240: easy consequence of the definition and the motivation for much of the field of proof complexity.
  :4241: 
  :4242: Theorem 21.4
  :4243: A proof system M in which SAT has polynomial proof complexity exists iff NP = coNP.
  :4244: 
  :4245: Many branches of mathematics, including logic, algebra, geometry, etc. give rise to proof sys-
  :4246: tems. Algorithms for SAT and automated theorem provers (popular in some areas of computer
  :4247: science) also may be viewed as proof systems.

  :4263: Chapter 22
  :4264: 
  :4265: Why are circuit lowerbounds so
  :4266: difficult?
  :4267: 
  :4268: Why have we not been able to prove strong lower bounds for circuits? In 1994 Razborov and Rudich
  :4269: formalized the notion of a "natural mathematical proof," for a circuit lowerbound. They pointed out
  :4270: that current lowerbound arguments involve "natural" mathematical proofs, and show that obtaining
  :4271: strong lowerbound with such techniques would violate a widely believed cryptographic assumption
  :4272: (namely, that factoring integers requires time 2n for some fixed > 0). Thus presumably we
  :4273: need to develop mathematical arguments that are not natural. This result may be viewed as a
  :4274: modern analogue of the Baker, Gill, Solovay result from the 1970s (see Chapter ??) that showed
  :4275: that diagonalization alone cannot resolve P versus NP and other questions.
  :4276: 
  :4277: Basically, a natural technique is one that proves a lowerbound for a random function and is
  :4278: "constructive." We formalize "constructive" later but first consider why lowerbound proofs may
  :4279: need to work for random functions.
  :4280: 
  :4281: 22.1 Formal Complexity Measures
  :4282: 
  :4283: Let us imagine at a high level how one might approach the project of proving circuit lower bounds.
  :4284: 
  :4285: For concreteness, focus on formulas, which are boolean circuits where gates have indegree 2 and
  :4286: 
  :4287: outdegree 1. It is tempting to use some kind of induction. Suppose we have a function like the one
  :4288: 
  :4289: in Figure 22.1 that we believe to be "complicated." Since the function computed at the output is
  :4290: 
  :4291: "complicated", intuition says that at least one of the functions on the incoming edges to the output
  :4292: 
  :4293: gate should also be "pretty complicated" (after all those two functions can be combined with a
  :4294: 
  :4295: single gate to produce a "complicated" function). Now we try to formalize this intuition, and point
  :4296: 
  :4297: out why one ends up proving a lowerbound on the formula complexity of random functions.
  :4298: 
  :4299: The most obvious way to formalize a "complicatedness" is as a function � that maps every
  :4300: boolean function on {0, 1}n to a nonnegative integer. (The input to � is the truth table of the
  :4301: 
  :4302: function.) We say that � is a formal complexity measure if it satisfies the following properties:
  :4303: 
  :4304: First, the measure is low for trivial functions: �(xi)  1 and �(x�i)  1 for all i. Second, we require
  :4305:

  :4331: Thus to formalize the inductive approach outlined earlier, it suffices to define a measure � such
  :4332: that �(CLIQUE) is high (say superpolynomial). For example, one could try "fraction of inputs for
  :4333: which the function agrees with the CLIQUE function" or some suitably modified version of this. In
  :4334: general, one imagines that defining a measure that lets us prove a good lowerbound for CLIQUE
  :4335: would involve some deep observation about the CLIQUE function. The next lemma seems to show,
  :4336: however, that even though all we care about is the CLIQUE function, our lowerbound necessarily
  :4337: must reason about random functions.
  :4338: 
  :4339: Lemma 22.2
  :4340: Suppose � is a formal complexity measure and there exists a function f : {0, 1}n  {0, 1} such

  :4344: Proof: Let g : {0, 1}n  {0, 1} be any function. Write f as f = h  g where h = f  g. So

  :4365: 22.2. NATURAL PROPERTIES          p22.3 (439)
  :4366: 
  :4367: 22.2 Natural Properties
  :4368: 
  :4369: Moving the above discussion forward, we think of a lowerbound proof as identifying some property
  :4370: of "hard" functions that is not shared by "easy" functions.
  :4371: 
  :4372: Definition 22.4
  :4373: A property  is a map from boolean functions to {0, 1}. A P-natural property useful against P/poly
  :4374: is a property  such that:
  :4375: 
  :4376: 1. (f ) = 1 for at least a 1/2n fraction of all boolean functions on n bits (recall that there are
  :4377: 22n functions on n bits);
  :4378: 
  :4379: 2. (f ) = 1 implies that f  P/poly (or more concretely, that f has circuit complexity at least
  :4380: nlog n, say); and
  :4381: 
  :4382: 3.  is computable on n-bit functions in 2O(n) time (i.e., polynomial in the length of the function's
  :4383: truth table).
  :4384: 
  :4385: The term P-natural refers to requirement (3). The property is useful against P/poly because of
  :4386: 
  :4387: requirement (2). (Note that this requirement also ensures that  is not trivial, since it must be 0 for
  :4388: 
  :4389: functions in P/poly.) Requirement (1) corresponds to our above intuition that circuit lowerbounds
  :4390: 
  :4391: should prove the hardness of a random function.
  :4392: 
  :4393: By suitably modifying (2) and (3) we can analogously define, for any complexity class C1 and
  :4394: circuit class C2, a C1-natural property that is useful against circuit class C2. We emphasize that
  :4395: when the property is computed, the input is the truth table of a function, whose size is 2n. Thus
  :4396: a P-natural property is computed in time 2cn for some constant c > 1 and a PSPACE-natural
  :4397: property is computed in space 2cn.
  :4398: 
  :4399: Example 22.5
  :4400: The result that PARITY is not computable in AC0 (Section ??) involved the following steps. (a)
  :4401: Show that every AC0 circuit can be simplified by restricting at most n-n input bits so that it then
  :4402: 
  :4403: becomes a constant function. (b) Show that the PARITY function does not have this property.
  :4404: 
  :4405: Thus the natural property lurking in this proof is the following: (f ) = 1 iff for every way of
  :4406: 
  :4407: assigning values to at most n - n input bits the function does not become a constant function.
  :4408: Clearly, if (f ) = 1 then f  AC0, so f is useful against AC0. Furthermore,  can be computed in
  :4409: 2O(n) time -- just enumerate all possible choices for the subsets of variables and all ways of setting
  :4410: 
  :4411: them to 0/1. This running time is polynomial in the length of the truth-table, so  is P-natural.
  :4412: 
  :4413: Finally, requirement (1) is also met since almost all boolean functions satisfy (f ) = 1 (easy to
  :4414: 
  :4415: check using a simple probability calculation; left as exercise).
  :4416: Thinking further, we see that  is a AC0-natural property that is useful against AC0.
  :4417: 
  :4418: DRAFT Web draft 2007-01-08 21:59
  :4419: 
  :4420: p22.4 (440)                                                  22.2. NATURAL PROPERTIES
  :4421: 
  :4422: Example 22.6
  :4423: The lowerbound for ACC0 circuits described in Section ?? is not natural per se. Razborov and
  :4424: 
  :4425: Rudich show how to naturalize the proof, in other words change it --while retaining its essence--so
  :4426: 
  :4427: that it does use a natural property. Recall that every boolean function on n bits can be represented
  :4428: 
  :4429: by a multilinear polynomial over GF (3). The space of all n-variate multilinear polynomials forms
  :4430: a vector space, whose dimension is N = 2n. Then all multilinear polynomials in n variables of total
  :4431: 
  :4432: degree less than n/2 form a subspace of dimension N/2 (this assumes n is even), and we denote this
  :4433: space by L. For a boolean function f let f^ be a multilinear polynomial over GF (3) that represents
  :4434: 
  :4435: f . Then define (F ) = 1 iff the dimension of the space
  :4436: 
  :4437: f^l1 + l2 : l1, l2  L
  :4438: 
  :4439: is at least 3N/4. It can be checked that  is 1 for the parity function, as well as for most ran-
  :4440: dom functions. Furthermore, rank computations can be done in NC2 so it is NC2-natural. The
  :4441: technique of Section ?? can be used to show that if (f ) = 1 then f  ACC0[3]; thus  is useful
  :4442: against ACC0[3].
  :4443: 
  :4444: Example 22.7
  :4445: The lowerbound for monotone circuits in Section ?? does use constructive methods, but it is
  :4446: challenging to show that it applies to a random function since a random function is not monotone.
  :4447: Nobody has formulated a good definition of a random monotone function.
  :4448: 
  :4449: In the definition of natural proofs, requirement (3) is the most controversial in that there is no
  :4450: inherent reason why mathematical proofs should go hand in hand with efficient algorithms.
  :4451: 
  :4452: Remark 22.8
  :4453: 
  :4454: "Constructive mathematics" was a movement within mathematics that rejected any proofs of exis-
  :4455: 
  :4456: tence that did not yield an algorithm for constructing the object. Today this viewpoint is considered
  :4457: 
  :4458: quaint; nonconstructive proofs are integral to mathematics.
  :4459: 
  :4460: In our context, "constructive" has a stricter meaning, namely the proof has to yield a polynomial-
  :4461: 
  :4462: time algorithm. Many proofs that would be "constructive" for a mathematician would be noncon-
  :4463: 
  :4464: structive under our definition. Surprisingly, even with this stricter definition, proofs in combinato-
  :4465: 
  :4466: rial mathematics are usually constructive, and --as Razborov and Rudich are pointing out --the
  :4467: 
  :4468: same is true of current circuit lowerbounds as well.
  :4469: 
  :4470: In a few cases, combinatorial results initially proved "nonconstructively" later turned out to
  :4471: 
  :4472: have constructive proofs: a famous example is the Lov`asz Local Lemma (discovered in 1974; al-
  :4473: 
  :4474: gorithmic version is in Beck [Bec91]). The same is true for several circuit lowerbounds--cf. the
  :4475: "naturalized" version of the Razborov-Smolensky lowerbound for ACC0[q] mentioned earlier, and
  :4476: 
  :4477: Raz's proof [Raz00] of the Babai-Nisan-Szegedy [BNS] lowerbound on multiparty communication
  :4478: 
  :4479: complexity.                                  Web draft 2007-01-08 21:59

  :4483: 22.3. LIMITATIONS OF NATURAL PROOFS  p22.5 (441)
  :4484: 
  :4485: 22.3 Limitations of Natural Proofs
  :4486: 
  :4487: The following theorem by Razborov and Rudich explains why we have not been able to use the
  :4488: same techniques to obtain an upper bound on P/poly: constructing a P-natural property useful
  :4489: against P/poly violates widely believed cryptographic assumptions.
  :4490: 
  :4491: Theorem 22.9 (Razborov, Rudich [RR97])
  :4492: Suppose a P-natural property  exists that is useful against P/poly. Then there are no strong
  :4493: pseudorandom function generators. In particular, FACTORING and DISCRETE LOG can be
  :4494: solved in less than 2n time for all > 0.
  :4495: 
  :4496: Pseudorandom function generators were defined in Section ??. The definition used a distin-
  :4497: guisher polynomial-time machine that is given oracle access to either a truly random function or a
  :4498: function from the pseudorandom family. The family is termed pseudorandom if the distinguisher
  :4499: cannot distinguish between the two oracles. Now we tailor that more general definition for our nar-
  :4500: row purposes in this section. We allow the distinguisher 2O(n) time and even allow it to examine the
  :4501: truth table of the function! This is without loss of generality since in 2O(n) time the distinguisher
  :4502: could construct the truth table using 2n queries to the oracle.
  :4503: 
  :4504: Definition 22.10
  :4505: A pseudorandom function generator is a function f (k, x) computable in polynomial time where the
  :4506: input x has n bits and the "key" k has nc bits, where c > 2 is a fixed constant. Denoting by Fn
  :4507: the function obtained by uniformly selecting k  {0, 1}nc and setting Fn to f (k, �), we have the
  :4508: property that the function ensemble F = {Fn}n=1 is "pseudorandom," namely, for each Turing
  :4509: machine M running in time 2O(n), and for all sufficiently large n,
  :4510: 
  :4511: 1
  :4512: | Pr[M (Fn) = 1] - Pr[M (Hn) = 1]| < 2n2 ,
  :4513: 
  :4514: where Hn is a random function on {0, 1}n.
  :4515: We will denote f (k, �) by fk.
  :4516: 
  :4517: Intuitively, the above definition says that if f is a pseudorandom function generator, then for
  :4518: a random k, the probability is high that fk "looks like a random function" to all Turing machines
  :4519: running in time 2O(n). Note that fk cannot look random to machines that run in 2O(nc) time since
  :4520: they can just guess the key k. Thus restricting the running time to 2O(n) (or to some other fixed
  :4521: exponential function such as 2O(n2)) is crucial.
  :4522: 
  :4523: Recall that Section ?? described the Goldreich-Goldwasser-Micali construction of pseudorandom
  :4524: function generators f (k, x) using a pseudorandom generator g that stretches nc random bits to 2nc
  :4525: pseudorandom (also see Figure 22.2): Let g0(k) and g1(k) denote, respectively, the first and last
  :4526: nc bits of g(k). Then the following function is a pseudorandom function generator, where MSB(x)
  :4527: refers to the first bit of a string x:
  :4528: 
  :4529: f (k, x) = MSB(gxn  gxn-1  � � �  gx2  gx1 (k)).
  :4530: 
  :4531: The exercises in Chapter 10 explored the security of this construction as a function of the
  :4532: 
  :4533: DRAFT security parameter of g; basically, the two are essentially the same. By the Goldreich-Levin theorem
  :4534: Web draft 2007-01-08 21:59
  :4535: 
  :4536: p22.6 (442)                                             22.4. MY PERSONAL VIEW
  :4537: Figure unavailable in pdf file.
  :4538: 
  :4539: Figure 22.2: Constructing a pseudorandom function generator from a pseudorandom generator.
  :4540: 
  :4541: of Section ??, a pseudorandom generator with such a high security parameter exists if a oneway
  :4542: permutation exists and some > 0, such that every 2n time algorithm has inversion probability
  :4543: less than 2-n . The DISCRETE LOG function --a permutation-- is conjectured to satisfy this
  :4544: property. As mentioned in Chapter 10, researchers believe that there is a small > 0 such that the
  :4545: worst-case complexity of DISCRETE LOG is 2n , which by random self-reducibility also implies the
  :4546: hardness of the average case. (One can also obtain pseudorandom generators using FACTORING,
  :4547: versions of which are also believed to be just as hard as DISCRETE LOG.) If this belief is correct,
  :4548: then pseudorandom function generators exist as outlined above. (Exercise.)

  :4550: Now we can prove the above theorem.

  :4563: 
  :4564: 22.4 My personal view
  :4565: 
  :4566: Discouraged by the Razborov-Rudich result, researchers (myself included) hardly ever work on
  :4567: circuit lowerbounds. Lately, I have begun to think this reaction was extreme. I still agree that
  :4568: a circuit lowerbound for say CLIQUE, if and when we prove it, will very likely apply to random
  :4569: functions as well. Thus the way to get around the Razborov-Rudich observation is to define
  :4570: properties that are not P-natural; in other words, are nonconstructive. I feel that this need not be
  :4571: such an insurmountable barrier since a host of mathematical results are nonconstructive.
  :4572: 
  :4573: Concretely, consider the question of separating NEXP from ACC0, one of the (admittedly
  :4574: not very ambitious) frontiers of circuit complexity outlined in Chapter 13. As observed there,
  :4575: NEXP = ACC0 will follow if we can improve the Babai-Nisan-Szegedy lowerbound of (n/2k)
  :4576: for k-party communication complexity to (n/poly(k)) for some function in NEXP. One line of
  :4577: attack is to lowerbound the discrepancy of all large cylinder intersections in the truth table, as we
  :4578: saw in Raz's proof of the BNS lowerbound1. (In other words, the "unnatural" property we are
  :4579: defining is  where (f ) = 1 iff f has high discrepancy and thus high multiparty communication
  :4580: complexity.) For a long time, I found this question intimidating because the problem of computing
  :4581: the discrepancy given the truth table of the function is coNP-hard (even for k = 2). This seemed
  :4582: 
  :4583: 1Interestingly, Raz discovered this naturalization of the BNS proof after being briefly hopeful that the original
  :4584: 
  :4585: DRAFT BNS proof--which is not natural-- may allow a way around the Razborov-Rudich result.
  :4586: Web draft 2007-01-08 21:59
  :4587: 
  :4588: 22.4. MY PERSONAL VIEW                                                            p22.7 (443)
  :4589: 
  :4590: to suggest that a proof that the discrepancy is high for an explicit function (which presumably will
  :4591: also show that it is high for random functions) must have a nonconstructive nature, and hence will
  :4592: be very difficult. Lately, I have begun to suspect this intuition.
  :4593: 
  :4594: A relevant example is Lov`asz's lowerbound of the chromatic number of the Kneser graph [Lov78].
  :4595: Lowerbounding the chromatic number is coNP-complete in general. Lov`asz gives a topological
  :4596: proof (using the famous Borsuk-Ulam fixed point theorem) that determines the chromatic number of
  :4597: the Kneser graph exactly. From his proof one can indeed obtain an algorithm for solving chromatic
  :4598: number on all graphs([MZ02]) --but it runs in PSPACE for general graphs! So if this were a circuit
  :4599: lowerbound we could call it PSPACE-natural, and thus "nonconstructive." Nevertheless, Lov`asz's
  :4600: reasoning for the particular case of the Kneser graph is not overly complicated because the graph is
  :4601: highly symmetrical. This suggests we should not blindly trust the intuition that "nonconstructive
  :4602: difficult."
  :4603: 
  :4604: I fervently hope that the next generation of researchers will view the Razborov-Rudich theorem
  :4605: as a guide rather than as a big obstacle!

  :4631: Chapter notes and history
  :4632: 
  :4633: The observation that circuit lowerbounds may unwittingly end up reasoning about random functions
  :4634: 
  :4635: DRAFT first appears in Razborov [Raz89]'s result about the limitations of the method of approximation.
  :4636: Web draft 2007-01-08 21:59
  :4637: 
  :4638: p22.8 (444)  22.4. MY PERSONAL VIEW
  :4639: 
  :4640: We did not cover the full spectrum of ideas in the Razborov-Rudich paper [RR97], where it is
  :4641: observed that candidate pseudorandom function generators exist even in the class TC0, which lies
  :4642: between ACC0 and NC1. Thus natural proofs will probably not allow us to separate even TC0
  :4643: from P.
  :4644: 
  :4645: Razborov's observation about submodular measures in Problem 5 is important because many
  :4646: existing approaches for formula complexity use submodular measures; thus they will fail to even
  :4647: prove superlinear lowerbounds.
  :4648: 
  :4649: In contrast with my limited optimism, Razborov himself expresses (in the introduction to [Raz03])
  :4650: a view that the obstacle posed by the natural proofs observation is very serious. He observes that
  :4651: existing lowerbound approaches use weak theories of arithmetic such as Bounded Arithmetic. He
  :4652: conjectures that any circuit lowerbound attempt in such a logical system must be natural (and
  :4653: hence unlikely to work). But as I mentioned, several theorems even in discrete mathematics use
  :4654: reasoning (e.g., fixed point theorems like Borsuk-Ulam) that does not seem to be formalizable in
  :4655: Bounded Arithmetic. Thus is my reason for optimism.
  :4656: 
  :4657: However, somen other researchers are far more pessimistic: they fear that P versus NP may
  :4658: be independent of mathematics (say, of Zermelo-Fraenkel set theory). Razborov says that he has
  :4659: no intuition about this.
